Ray: Good morning, nerds! It's Friday, November sixth, twenty twenty-six, and this is Nerd News Radio.

Lead story

Ray: Okay, so the problem. Steel property models can score well on random test splits, even when they do badly on alloys they haven't seen before.

Ada: Right, because a random split puts close cousins of the same steel on both sides of the line.

Ray: That's the worry. The paper introduces SteelAgent, which pairs metallurgical descriptors and machine learning models with a language model interface. It handles property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. But the real focus is how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions, using SteelBench tensile strength evaluations.

Ada: So what did they actually measure?

Ray: For gradient boosting, the R squared, which is a score where one means perfect prediction, was zero point eight five nine on a random split. When whole steel families were held out, it dropped to zero point one one three.

Ada: Wow. That's basically a different model.

Ray: And the uncertainty took a hit too. Prediction intervals nominally meant to cover ninety percent of cases covered ninety-one percent under random splitting, but only thirty-seven point six percent on held-out sources.

Ada: So the model was confidently wrong. Did the physics-based features rescue it?

Ray: It depends on the evaluation. They raised R squared by zero point two five three four in a seventeen family holdout, but lowered it by zero point three five eight in a separate four grade laboratory analysis.

Ada: Okay, but is that real data or a toy? Because calibration failing could be a quirk.

Ray: They report group-level errors, and they also run a synthetic regression experiment to illustrate how calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups. So both real and synthetic, and they're labeled as such.

Ada: Does the abstract say how it fares in a real mill or lab?

Ray: It doesn't. What it does say is that estimates or compliance scores should be reported alongside the evaluation population. Honestly, that's a good habit for any materials model.

Magnets and materials

Ray: On to magnets. First, a theory paper on a spin supersolid in an easy-axis triangular antiferromagnet, using fermionic partons, which are a mathematical trick for splitting spins into simpler pieces.

Ada: And is this an experiment?

Ray: No, mean-field plus a random phase approximation calculation. Two states, called Y and Y prime, are degenerate classically. The mean-field energy favors Y prime, but fluctuation corrections can make Y lower. They also find a roton minimum and a gapped pseudo-Goldstone mode, which has been seen experimentally.

Ada: So experiments are the next test, then.

Ray: Next, a Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials paper on thermal stability of tetrataenite, an iron nickel phase pitched as a rare-earth-free magnet. Authors include Laura Lewis. We only have the byline, no abstract.

Ada: So we can't say what the stability limits are.

Ray: Correct. Third, a Monte Carlo idea: a discrete model that exactly reproduces the multichannel Kondo model, simulated with cluster algorithms that the authors say completely eliminate critical slowing down.

Ada: Which means simulations don't get stuck near a transition. Nice, but it's a methods result.

Ray: Exactly. Not a materials result yet.

Ray: Last one: scanning laser vibrometer data of welded parts, reconstructed with a complex-valued neural radiance field. Mean correlation at held-out angles was zero point six zero, versus zero point two eight for a baseline.

Ada: So welded aluminum parts, not powder bed printing.

Ray: Right. Nondestructive evaluation.

Weird physics corner

Ray: Okay, this one is wild. A paper proves that deciding whether a quantum Hamiltonian is frustration-free, meaning its ground state satisfies every local term at once, is decidable. There's a finite size cutoff that settles it for all sizes.

Steel ML model R² drops from 0.86 to 0.11 on held-out families

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

The abstract reports that a gradient-boosting model reached R² of 0.859 on a random split but only 0.113 when entire steel families were held out. Coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals also fell to 37.6% on held-out sources. It is a clear illustration that random splits can overstate how well a model generalizes.

Track-height control for DED on porous substrates uses system identification

arXiv · ML for manufacturing · 7/10

The abstract describes a conceptual approach: characterise the process dynamics with system identification, then test which control strategies suit the process. It concerns directed energy deposition (DED) rather than laser powder bed fusion, and the abstract reports no experimental results. It matters for anyone interested in closed-loop control of metal additive manufacturing.

Spin-orbit-locked symmetry keeps triangular Dirac spin liquid stable in Yb delafossites

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract reports that symmetry forbids every Dirac mass, density and current at any order. Bond-dependent exchange couplings (J±± and J_z±) are locked to the lattice by spin-orbit coupling, giving a worked example of which anisotropic couplings it can generate. A companion paper covers the same ground, and the selection of the chiral-Ising class by easy-plane anisotropy is the claim to watch.

2D Ising model on hyperbolic lattices: boundary conditions change the scaling

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract reports worm and Metropolis simulations in which open boundaries give non-mean-field finite-size scaling exponents, while wired boundaries give a mean-field magnetization exponent. It also reports substantial finite-size effects in the Binder crossings and susceptibility peaks, a reminder that small simulations can mislead.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Spin supersolid in easy-axis triangular antiferromagnet via fermionic partons

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports a parton mean-field plus RPA study of the easy-axis XXZ triangular antiferromagnet. The Y and Y' states are degenerate classically, and the mean-field energy favors Y', showing how easy-axis anisotropy shapes the ordered state. It is theory only, so experimental evidence would be the next test.

Thermal stability of tetrataenite (L1₀ FeNi) for rare-earth-free magnets

J. Magnetism & Magnetic Materials · 6/10

No abstract was available, so the details are unconfirmed. Tetrataenite is a candidate rare-earth-free permanent magnet with strong uniaxial anisotropy, and its thermal stability limits are the key quantitative question the paper addresses.

Cluster Monte Carlo removes critical slowing down in the Kondo model

Physical Review Letters · 6/10

The abstract reports a discrete model that reproduces the multichannel Kondo model exactly and is simulated with cluster algorithms. The authors claim the approach eliminates critical slowing down completely. It is a Monte Carlo methods idea rather than a materials result.

Transient resetting speeds relaxation near a first-order transition

Physical Review Letters · 6/10

The abstract reports that brief stochastic resets accelerate relaxation to the stationary state, sometimes exponentially, in a Mpemba-like way. The protocol needs only macroscopic properties such as the order parameter. The setting is quantum many-body, so transfer to classical dynamics is not shown.

Additive Manufacturing

Pulsed-arc printing makes meter-tall titanium single crystals

3D Printing Industry · 6/10

A 3D Printing Industry story says a Nature study from groups in China and the US prints titanium alloy single crystals a meter tall. It is a notable metal additive manufacturing result, though it concerns grain structure more than process monitoring.

Neural rendering of laser-vibrometer scans for defect detection

arXiv · ML for manufacturing · 3/10

The abstract reports a complex-valued NeRF variant with a mean ZNCC of 0.60 at held-out viewing angles, against 0.28 for a baseline. It applies to nondestructive evaluation of welded parts rather than in-situ laser powder bed fusion monitoring, and the abstract says only that the reconstructions supported defect detection.

Learned single-pixel illumination patterns for weld radiograph classification

arXiv · ML for manufacturing · 3/10

The abstract reports that learned illumination patterns beat the best fixed transform by 9-15 points at 8 measurements, across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and the RIAWELC weld dataset. It is a sensing-efficiency idea, and the advantage shrinks as the measurement budget grows. It does not use laser powder bed fusion data.

Theoretical Physics

Reentrant skyrmion phase appears under oscillating fields in Monte Carlo

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 7/10

The abstract reports Monte Carlo simulations of a 2D Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya magnet in a periodic field. A skyrmion phase with no equilibrium counterpart appears between the skyrmion and polarized phases, and higher driving frequencies suppress it.

Anti-spin ice realized with attracting particles

Phys.org · General physics · 6/10

A Nature Communications study reports an anti-spin ice built from attracting particles that breaks the ice rule governing conventional spin ices. Spin ice is a frustrated magnet in which each tetrahedron obeys a two-in, two-out local rule, and here that rule is deliberately violated. Only a summary is available, so details are unconfirmed.

Frustration-freeness is decidable but unprovable in standard mathematics

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 6/10

A Hamiltonian is frustration-free if its ground state satisfies every local term at once, as in the AKLT and toric-code models. The abstract proves a finite system-size cutoff settles the question for all sizes, but that cutoff is uncomputable. It also exhibits a Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness cannot be proved in ZFC, tying a concrete many-body question to the limits of logic.

Proposal to test whether gravity entangles a particle with nuclear clocks

arXiv · quantum physics · 6/10

The proposal asks whether gravity can entangle a levitated micrometer-scale particle with an array of nuclear clocks. The abstract says this would test whether internal clock energy contributes to active gravitational mass, something no prior experiment has tested. It is a proposal, not a measurement, and it sits inside a live debate about whether gravity is quantum.

Rare-earth truce extended, but legal deadlines stand

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 7/10

The Environmental Leader headline says a rare-earth truce has been extended while its legal deadlines remain in place. Only the headline is available, so the specifics are unconfirmed. It bears on the supply-risk debate around magnets.

Colorado rare-earth bid targets China's estimated 94% magnet share

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 7/10

Rocky Mountain Voice reports a Colorado bid aimed at China's estimated 94% hold on permanent magnets. Only the headline is available. It adds context for why magnets that rely less on rare earths are getting attention, and the 94% figure is an estimate.

US rare-earth project eyes 4x output of magnetic material

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 6/10

Interesting Engineering describes a US project targeting about 6,000 tons of critical magnetic material and four times the output. Only the headline is available, so timelines and funding are unconfirmed. It points to domestic magnet capacity scaling up.

DOE announces $67M for manufacturing competitiveness

News · AM policy & funding · 5/10

The DOE announcement gives no detail on scope in the headline. Whether additive manufacturing is eligible is unknown from the headline alone, so the DOE page is the place to confirm.
